Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

# Labour Party Manifesto 2005: Summary

## Core Vision

New Labour's 2005 manifesto centers on a fundamental proposition: government's duty is to provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. The document positions Labour as breaking down barriers, extending opportunity nationwide, and building safe communities for law-abiding citizens. The manifesto explicitly frames choices as "forward not back"—rejecting Conservative approaches while embedding a "new progressive consensus."

## Economic Framework

Labour claims an unprecedented economic record: the longest uninterrupted growth period, lowest sustained inflation since the 1960s, and two million additional jobs. The party commits to maintaining economic stability through Bank of England independence, the two percent inflation target, and fiscal responsibility—borrowing only to invest while keeping debt prudent.

The manifesto rejects "false choices" between economic dynamism and social justice, arguing both must advance together. Labour pledges not to raise basic or top income tax rates, nor extend VAT to essentials. The goal is "full employment in every region"—targeting an 80% employment rate through New Deal programs, tax credits, and welfare reform including Incapacity Benefit changes requiring most claimants to engage in work-focused activities.

## Education: Personalized Learning

Education remains Labour's "number one priority." The document celebrates international rankings (third globally for literacy at age ten) while pledging to tailor education to individual needs. Key commitments include:

- Every secondary school becoming an independent specialist school
- 200 Academies by 2010 in underperforming communities
- 15-year Building Schools for the Future programme
- Expanding sixth-form, college, and apprenticeship places
- Maintaining the 50% higher education participation target
- Capping tuition fees at £3,000 (inflation-adjusted) throughout the Parliament

The manifesto emphasizes discipline—"no child has the right to disrupt others' education"—while promising enhanced special educational needs support.

## Healthcare: NHS Transformation

Healthcare policy rests on the principle that "access to treatment should be based on clinical need not ability to pay." Labour touts doubled NHS spending since 1997, with plans for tripled funding by 2008. Waiting time targets are central: maximum 18 weeks from referral to treatment by 2008, with patient choice of hospital.

The party embraces "innovation and reform" through independent sector provision, NHS Foundation Trusts, and expanded primary care services—while emphasizing these remain "free at the point of need with no charges for hospital operations." Healthy living initiatives include school meal reforms, smoking restrictions (banning smoking in workplaces and restaurants while allowing some pubs to choose), and obesity prevention measures.

## Crime and Security

The manifesto claims overall crime down 30%—"almost five million fewer crimes a year." Labour pledges neighborhood policing teams for every community, 24,000 Community Support Officers, and continued tough action on antisocial behavior through ASBOs and fixed penalty notices.

Controversially, the document commits to introducing ID cards "backed up by a national register," initially voluntary as passports are renewed. Immigration policy introduces a points-based system prioritizing skilled workers, with fingerprinting requirements for visa applicants and civil penalties for employers of illegal workers.

On terrorism, Labour defends its record including the Iraq war while acknowledging disagreement: "Many people disagreed with the action we took in Iraq. We respect and understand their views." However, the party maintains troops should remain "under a United Nations mandate as long as the democratically elected government there wants them."

## Social Justice Agenda

The manifesto commits to ending child poverty "starting by halving it by 2010-11." Family policy includes extended paid maternity leave (nine months by 2007, targeting a full year), universal childcare through 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres, and expanded flexible working rights.

For pensioners, Labour highlights the Pension Credit guaranteeing minimum £109 weekly income, increased Winter Fuel Payments, and free local bus travel for over-60s. The party seeks "national consensus" on long-term pension reform while addressing women's disadvantages in the system.

## Constitutional Reform

Labour promises completing House of Lords reform, removing remaining hereditary peers while allowing a free vote on composition. Devolution continues with enhanced Welsh Assembly powers and London Mayor responsibilities reviewed. The manifesto emphasizes "strong local government" with reduced bureaucracy and greater council freedoms, while neighborhood-level powers address local concerns like graffiti and antisocial behavior.

## International Leadership

Britain's G8 presidency focuses on climate change and African poverty. Labour commits to the UN's 0.7% development aid target by 2013 and "100 percent debt relief for the poorest." The party supports the EU Constitutional Treaty, pledging a referendum while campaigning for "Yes."

The manifesto maintains commitment to the independent nuclear deterrent while emphasizing multilateral approaches to proliferation. On Europe, Labour presents membership as essential for "jobs, trade and prosperity" while promising to reform EU regulation and agricultural subsidies.

Throughout, the document weaves together economic competence with social justice, individual responsibility with collective provision, and national strength with international engagement—the defining synthesis of the New Labour project.

# Green Party Manifesto 2005: Summary

## A Vision for Sustainable Society

The Green Party presents a comprehensive programme built on social, economic and environmental justice, placing people and planetary resources at the heart of policy. The manifesto challenges the Westminster status quo, which has created widening inequality, eroded public services, and ignored environmental destruction.

## Economic Transformation

The Greens propose radical economic reform, arguing that current stability rests on short-term wealth creation, resource overuse, and gross inequality. Their approach treats natural resources as finite capital rather than disposable income, implementing progressive taxation with higher rates for top earners (50% above £50,000, 60% above £100,000). VAT would be replaced with eco-taxes reflecting environmental costs. The party champions economic localisation over globalisation, supporting community banks, credit unions, and local currencies whilst opposing euro membership. A Citizen's Income and Citizen's Pension would provide universal security, reducing means-testing and empowering individuals.

## Climate Change and Energy

Climate change represents the gravest environmental and economic threat. The Greens adopt the Contraction and Convergence framework, targeting 20% carbon reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. This includes carbon taxation, 40% renewable energy by 2020, and closure of nuclear power stations. A Warmer Homes Act would reduce domestic energy demand by 30%.

## Public Services

The manifesto demands restoration of the NHS to founding principles—comprehensive, universal care based on need—rejecting privatisation, foundation hospitals, and Public-Private Partnerships. Health funding would rise to EU average levels. Education policy includes scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, abolishing SATs, and introducing individualised learning.

## Transport Revolution

Transport policy prioritises sustainable modes: walking, cycling, and public transport over private cars and aviation. Rail and tube networks would return to public ownership. Motoring would reflect true environmental costs through congestion charging and fuel duties, while aviation fuel taxation would end the industry's effective £9 billion annual subsidy.

## Environmental Protection

A Zero Waste Strategy would outlaw incineration and target 60% recycling by 2010. The precautionary principle would govern new technologies including genetic modification. Animal rights would be extended, with bans on blood sports, battery cages, and live exports.

## Food and Farming

The Organics Target Bill would achieve 30% organic production by 2012. The Common Agricultural Policy, promoting unsustainable industrialised farming, would be replaced with support for local food markets and smaller farms. Genetically modified food would be banned.

## Crime and Communities

Crime reduction focuses on prevention through strong communities, improved urban design, youth facilities, and addressing social causes. Community policing would increase, with restorative justice central to the system. Strict gun control legislation would be implemented, whilst national ID cards are opposed.

## Democratic Renewal

Constitutional reform would devolve power to local communities, introduce proportional representation, and create an elected House of Lords. The proposed EU constitution fails democratic and sustainability tests; the Greens campaign for rejection whilst remaining committed to European engagement.

## International Justice

A truly ethical foreign policy would replace militarism with peaceful diplomacy. UK nuclear weapons would be decommissioned, arms sales ended, and overseas aid increased to 1% of GNI. Debt cancellation for the 52 poorest countries would promote stability. The World Trade Organisation would be reformed through a General Agreement on Sustainable Trade, favouring local economies over corporate globalisation. Asylum seekers would receive proper support and rights under international conventions.

The manifesto represents a political programme for the next hundred years, not merely the next hundred days—offering real choice for real change.
